t: Who Else But Us
q: It's profoundly misguided for me to assume that I can make claims about what is and isn't valued in a student's home. I've been doing this long enough to have many, many students and families surprise me by revealing things, months or years into knowing them.
Basically, folks are complex; homes and families, even more so. We're better off with a humbler, "I know less than I think" kind of stance toward our students' homes.

There is no one else in the lives of my students more responsible for cultivating Value for learning in my subject area, during the year that my students are with me, than I am. No one is more responsible. No one is better equipped.
This doesn't mean it's our fault if students don't come to value learning while they're with us. It just means that it's our fault if we don't relentlessly aim to bring this increase in Value about.

But regardless of what happens at home, the good news is that the realm I control is powerful. In my classroom — and in yours — there can be grown the kind of life-giving counter-culture where learning is good because it's good.

t: How do the parts fit the whole?- the role of seemingly vague facts ly-vague-facts/
q: To make the thread running through a course become apparent to our novice learners, we have to reiterate the significance and links connecting a seemingly vague fact to other ideas/facts.

One mistake that I would make is to not explain the significance of all relevant structures in a cell to processes. Sure, I would say that a certain structure does a certain job and that would be that. There was no actual meaning to it.
When teaching the cell membrane initially, I make sure to suggest that substances need a way to pass through and not just to say that is its job. I am planting a seed that I will return to later.
The cell membrane has a role to play in many major processes but its very structure enables certain processes to happen at increased rates.

Here, I explain that microvilli are folds or protusions of the cell membrane of the cells that make up the villi. Having the larger surface area means more digested food molecules can pass through quickly. This makes the rate of diffusion higher and the whole thing very efficient.

None of this takes a lot of time. In fact, in some cases, many teachers already mention the cell membrane. But this is more about attaching meaning to its function and not just relaying the definition each time.

A similar process can be followed when teaching the cytoplasm. For instance, when teaching enzymes, focusing on the fact that many of them work in the cytoplasm of cells makes it a centre of activity, and not just blank space.

t: The Behavior Illusion Of The First Weeks Of School
q: After the first two or three weeks of school you may be lulled into thinking that you have a great class.

Well, early in the school year students are on their best behavior. They’re attentive and excited. They’re eager and appreciative after a long, boring summer. Many are also trying to turn over a new leaf .
In this day and age, you’re never going to have a great class all on its own. Left to their own devices, your classroom will become Lord of the Flies. Just the way it is.

One day, however, it will catch up to you. The air will feel different. Subtle at first, perhaps, but it’s there. Hints of tension and excitability. Voices on edge. Tinges of disrespect, entitlement, and a slow but sure takeover of your classroom.

All those early halcyon days – if you’re lucky enough to even have them – are no more than an opportunity to set your classroom management plan and its sharply defined rules and consequences in stone.

t: Youthful Purpose Guru Bill Damon's Golden Opportunity
q: There's this researcher out of Stanford who basically dedicated his life to studying why some people enter adulthood with a strong sense of purpose and others don't.

One golden opportunity to [give young people purposeful role models] is for teachers to tell students why they chose teaching as a profession, what they find fulfilling about teaching and what they hope to accomplish with their students.
The point of doing this is not to persuade their students to become teachers but rather to show what it looks like for an admired adult to pursue a vocation with purpose.
It was a very striking moment for me because I didn't really like much what I had seen the doctor doing, and I wasn't really interested in medicine like I thought that I would be.

So it was a few months later when I went to a Boys and Girls Club in Chicago, and I got to work with all these young people there at the Club, and I just suddenly realized, 'Wow, this is really cool; I really like to work with young people.'

t: How to Have Fun Helping Your Students Value School This Year
q: When students don't optimally Value school, they'll say things like this: This is boring. This is pointless. Why do we have to do this?

Here's why: your classroom is an alternate world from the one your students normally inhabit. Or at least, it should be. It's a cosmos — Latinized from the Greek kosmos: a good order, an orderly arrangement; a world.

Whether you teach art or agriculture, social studies or Scripture, English language arts or personal finance, you are, day by day, through helping your students toward mastery of your discipline, inviting them in to a cosmos.

When your students respond to your high-impact lessons with moans and groans, this need not frighten or bother you. There's a way to become so sure of the goodness of what you have on offer in your cosmos that you don't bat an eye when folks are genuinely hesitant about its goodness.

t: A Critical Mistake Teachers Make On The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2022/08/05/mistake-teachers-make-the-first-day-of-school/
q: You see, there is a mistake teachers make during the window of time between teaching their plan and enforcing their plan.
But here’s the thing: You just got finished emphatically teaching your rules and consequences and explaining their supreme importance. You just promised to follow through no matter what.

But it’s a critical mistake. No matter how unpleasant it may seem at the time, if a student breaks a rule, you must enforce . There is no window of time. No grace period. No kinda-sorta easing into it.
The second you finish teaching your classroom management plan you must go live. You must send the message that you mean what you say. If a student misbehaves right away, you should celebrate.
When you don’t follow through you communicate to your new students that you’re a pushover who can’t be trusted, doesn’t mean what they say, and isn’t serious about classroom management.
x: Teaching a classroom management plan thoroughly is only half the job.
A common first-day mistake is hesitating or excusing the very first rule violation as a 'teachable moment' rather than enforcing the promised consequence.
There is no legitimate grace period or transition window once a classroom management plan has been taught; enforcement must begin immediately.

q: And here, colleague, is through line number one: the inner work of the teacher. It's a thing. It's a skill. It's a muscle. Grow it, and delight. Neglect it, and pine.
Set simple rules that place boundaries around your working hours this coming school year. Here are mine.
Monday through Friday: I can work from whenever I wake up until I need to be home from work, which is 5:00 or 5:30 pm depending on the night's agenda. And do no work at home!
As I discuss in the video — these work for me and my family. They're not better or worse than yours. Whatever your constraints are, my encouragement to you is to accept and embrace them.
Communicate these rules with someone who will hold you accountable. Be prepared for these rules to cause you problems, and please — let these problems help you!

q: What, in a single sentence, is your Everest this school year? If you had to boil down into a single sentence what you're hoping your class/classes/subjects produce in your students, what would that sentence be?

What one area of professional growth would you like to focus on this school year? This makes way for what I've previously called lumpy growth, and it's the most motivating method I'm aware of for growing in your expertise as a teacher.
Through teaching music and band, I can help my students become good citizens. "Good" meaning kind, responsible, problem solvers, and hard workers.

I hope that students are able to see that learning a language is a pathway to better understanding others and themselves — to learn to communicate with others who may be different from them and who may see the world through a different lens allows them to understand the world at a deeper level.
It's my contention that, while there are tons of things we can pick to improve upon as teachers, these are some of the areas that most impact our Credibility with students.
